title: Service Fidelity, Cost Tradeoffs, and SLO Matrix Framework
author: Maya Chen
content:
Overview

This document defines a pragmatic framework for reasoning about service fidelity, per-request cost, and SLO placement across Redwood Inference's serving surface. It codifies a matrix for mapping request classes to SLO/budget pairs, prescribes API-level hints to enable runtime cost/fidelity negotiation, and provides an operational rollout and measurement playbook. The goal is to make tradeoffs repeatable, observable, and reversible.

Why this exists (Motivation)

- Rising model heterogeneity (full-precision, quantized, distilled variants) and multi-modal endpoints demand explicit guidance on when to sacrifice fidelity to save cost.
- Customers require predictable unit economics; teams need standard controls for graceful quality degradation under constrained capacity.
- Existing standards cover SLOs and fallback but do not specify a cross-cutting mapping from request intent -> fidelity budget -> runtime config.

Scope

- Applies to all Redwood runtime surfaces: Hosted API, Dedicated pools, and Private deployments.
- Targets text generation, chat sessions, and embedding requests. Does not change model artifacts or evaluation standards; it augments serving and API semantics.

Definitions

- Fidelity tier: qualitative label representing expected output quality (e.g., "high-precision", "balanced", "fast-safe").
- Cost budget: expected token or GPU cost per request (USD/normalized-unit) or a relative multiplier.
- Request class: classification of a call by business intent (e.g., transactional, exploratory, background-batch).
- Negotiation hint: API-level field that signals client preference along latency/cost/fidelity axes.

Principles

1. Observable tradeoffs: Every degradation must have an associated metric (quality SLI) and cost delta.
2. Testable fallbacks: Fallback variants must be regression-tested against a pinned prompt-set and primed with the same acceptance criteria as the primary variant.
3. Runtime reversibility: Any runtime policy that reduces fidelity must be reversible via feature flags or rollout controls without model artifact changes.
4. Minimal client burden: Clients express preferences via small, orthogonal fields; runtime decides exact variant.

SLO / Fidelity Matrix (reference)

This matrix maps request classes to desired SLOs and budget windows. Teams must adopt the nearest matching row as their default and justify deviations in a short RFC.

Request class | Expected latency p95 | Quality SLI (acceptance) | Fidelity tier | Cost budget (relative) | Typical runtime action
---|---:|---:|---|---:|---
Transaction (user-facing) | < 150ms | >= 98% on golden prompt-set | high-precision | 1.0x | Pin full-precision model, avoid quantization, use low-batch, KV-cache hot path
Conversational (session) | < 300ms | >= 95% compr. over session | balanced | 0.8x | Balanced quantization, small batching, session-aware KV warming
Exploratory (search/ideation) | < 500ms | >= 90% diversity+coherency | balanced-fast | 0.6x | Use distilled or quantized variant, enable prefix-caching
Background-batch (async) | best-effort | >= 85% pass rate on eval-set | fast-safe | 0.2-0.4x | Max batching, relaxed latency, heavy quantization, Dedicated pools
Diagnostic / Debug | best-effort | metrics not enforced | developer-debug | variable | Route to non-production flavors, enable extra tracing

Note: the Cost budget column is a relative multiplier versus the canonical high-precision configuration. Teams must maintain a documented mapping between the multiplier and the absolute unit pricing for their deployment mode.

API-level Negotiation Hints (contract)

We extend the request schema with three optional fields. Backwards compatibility guarantee: default behavior equals existing production semantics (high-precision for customer requests).

- fidelity_hint: one of ["high", "balanced", "economy"] (string) - soft preference.
- max_cost_multiplier: decimal string (e.g., "0.6") - hard budget cap. When present, runtime must not select a configuration that exceeds this multiplier.
- latency_priority: one of ["low", "medium", "high"] - indicates acceptable latency sensitivity.

Example request snippet (JSON):

{
  "input": "Summarize the document...",
  "fidelity_hint": "economy",
  "max_cost_multiplier": "0.5",
  "latency_priority": "low"
}

Runtime Interpretation Rules

1. If max_cost_multiplier is present, treat it as authoritative and choose the cheapest configuration that meets the request class acceptance SLI where possible.
2. fidelity_hint is advisory and used to break ties or allow slightly higher cost for quality-sensitive calls.
3. latency_priority overrides batching heuristics: "high" attempts to reduce batch windows at the expense of cost.

Model Variant Selection Algorithm (summary)

1. Resolve request class (from client header or routing policy).
2. Apply tenant-level policy overrides (enterprise customers may lock fidelity tiers).
3. If max_cost_multiplier present, filter variants to those below threshold.
4. Score remaining variants by expected quality delta + latency delta + cold-start risk. Use weighted sum: 0.5*quality_score + 0.3*latency_score + 0.2*cold_start_penalty.
5. Select top variant; incrementally sample a small percentage for higher-fidelity variants for ongoing validation.

Configuration Table (recommended keys and defaults)

key | type | default | description
runtime.default_fidelity | string | "balanced" | default fidelity for the service if client omits hints
runtime.cost_multiplier_map | yaml | see below | maps fidelity tiers to relative cost multipliers
runtime.max_batch_ms | int | 8 | default maximum batching window in ms for interactive traffic
runtime.kv_warm_threshold | int | 3 | number of session requests to mark a session for KV prewarm
runtime.sampling_rate_high_fidelity | float | 0.01 | fraction of requests forcibly sent to higher fidelity for validation

Example cost mapping (YAML text stored as config value):

runtime.cost_multiplier_map:
  high: 1.0
  balanced: 0.8
  economy: 0.45

Acceptance criteria and metrics

Every service that adopts the framework must publish the following metrics to the Redwood telemetry pipeline (labels: service, environment, fidelity_tier):

- fidelity_acceptance_rate: fraction of sampled prompts passing the golden prompt-set acceptance thresholds per fidelity tier.
- cost_per_request (normalized): measured token/GPU cost normalized to high-precision baseline.
- p95_latency_ms: 95th percentile latency.
- fallback_rate: fraction of requests where runtime downgraded fidelity due to capacity.
- quality_regression_alerts: counts of surfaced regressions from continuous eval.

Deployment and Rollout Playbook

1. Design: author a short RFC describing the default row in the SLO matrix and any tenant-specific overrides. Include the golden prompt-set used for acceptance tests.
2. Staging: enable negotiation hints in staging, run a 7-day smoke with sampling_rate_high_fidelity=0.2. Verify fidelity_acceptance_rate >= target.
3. Canary: Gradually route 5/25/50/100% of production traffic to the new policy with automated checks: cost_per_request within expected band (±15%), no new quality_regression_alerts.
4. Full rollout: enable feature flags to flip default runtime.default_fidelity. Keep sampling at 1% for 14 days for sanity.
5. Rollback: feature-flag driven; if any of the automated checks fail for 30m sustained, revert to previous default and open an incident.

Operational runbook (incident quick steps)

- Symptom: sudden spike in quality_regression_alerts or customer complaints.
- Triage steps: 
  1. Check recent deploys and feature-flag changes.
  2. Inspect recent changes to runtime.cost_multiplier_map and sampling_rate_high_fidelity.
  3. If a rollback is indicated, flip runtime.default_fidelity to previous stable value and increase sampling to 100% for 15 minutes to validate.
  4. Notify affected customers and create a postmortem if >1% traffic affected.

Ownership and Governance

- Author: Maya Chen (Platform Performance) - primary author and steward for the first-year rollout.
- Runtime maintainers: eng-serving-runtime (oncall: runtime-shift).
- Compliance steward: security-and-compliance to verify privacy of any sampled prompts.
- Product sign-off: Product PM owning the service must approve the chosen SLO matrix row.

Open questions and future work

- Should we expose a fine-grained numerical cost_budget field (micro-cents) rather than multiplier? Pros: precise control. Cons: increases client complexity.
- Integration with Optimize: can we provide per-tenant automated recommendations for default_fidelity based on historical cost/quality curves?
- How to standardize golden prompt-sets across teams without leaking customer prompts? Consider anonymous, synthetic prompt-generation guidelines.

Appendix: Example SLO config (service-level)

{
  "service": "text-summarizer",
  "default_fidelity": "balanced",
  "slo": {
    "latency_p95_ms": 300,
    "fidelity_acceptance": 0.95,
    "cost_multiplier_target": 0.8
  },
  "runtime": {
    "sampling_rate_high_fidelity": 0.01,
    "max_batch_ms": 8
  }
}
